tests.description: Reference: WRF 4.8 em_scm_xy COLD-SEASON single-column run, data/eqwefic/noahcold_scm, dumped by ctessum-claude/WRF branch earthsciml-instrumented-noahcold and replayed through the real64 (-fdefault-real-8) kernels/noah_driver at ESM_DT = 0.01 s. THE ASSERTIONS BY CLAIM. CLAIM 1, the liquid budget: `dsh2o_dt_total` per layer against WRF's own (sh2o_out - sh2o_in)/dt, plus its new term checked in its own right by `melt` (against SNOPAC's EX) and `water_supply` (against SNOPAC's PRCP1). CLAIM 2, the total-water budget: `dsmc_dt_total` and `dsice_dt`, which say that the phase change moves water between liquid and ice within a layer and does not change the total -- an error leaking transport into the phase term passes claim 1 and fails this. CLAIM 3, the switches at zero tolerance: `phase_active`, the frozen sink's clamp decision made at the assembly's shared state against WRF's at its post-SMFLX state, and `melting`, SNOPAC's own branch. PRECONDITION, not a result: `supersaturation_active` = 0. BOTH NEW EDGES ARE LOAD-BEARING, CHECKED BY BREAKING THEM. Removing the snowmelt coupling library turns 5 of these 20 assertions red; setting `dew_to_soil` back to its snow-free default of 1 turns 3 red on the frost column. A coupling that passes with its edge cut proves nothing, so both were cut. THE REFERENCE STEP, AND THE FIRST COLUMN WHERE THE BOUND IS PHYSICS RATHER THAN PRECISION. Worst absolute residual over this document's assertions: 4.53e-11 at ESM_DT = 1e-6 s, 4.64e-14 at 0.01 s, and 1.0 -- an INDICATOR FLIP -- at 60 s, where WRF's interval clamp changes decision in two layers (0 -> 2, stopped at `free`) and the phase term stops being a rate at all. That right-hand branch is not a smooth truncation error: it is a discrete switch, absent until it is catastrophic, which is why the V has to be measured rather than extrapolated. The left branch is the usual cancellation in the differenced reference and scales as 1/dt, so at 0.01 s it contributes 4.5e-15 -- close to the eps(sh2o)/dt = 6.7e-15 estimate. But the MEASURED residual there is 4.64e-14, about seven times that, and the excess is O(dt) rather than O(1/dt): it is the operator-splitting error itself. THIS IS THE FIRST OF THE FIVE FROZEN-COLUMN DOCUMENTS WHERE THE SPLITTING ERROR EXCEEDS THE REFERENCE FLOOR, and the reason is the melt: 8.0e-7 m/s of surface water against the bare-ground columns' 1e-9 m/s of dew, driving a nonlinear infiltration limiter, so WRF applying the transport before the sink and a continuous formulation applying them at one state no longer agree to round-off. 4.2e-14 of 3.9e-6 is 1.1e-8 relative -- small, but it is a real difference between the two formulations and not noise. The bound is 2e-13, four times the measured residual, and it is the SPLITTING error it is sized from, not the reference's precision. WHICH OF THE TWO SIZED THE BOUND: the OPERATOR-SPLITTING ERROR, not the reference's precision, and this is the first Noah bound of which that is true. The two bounds on a differenced reference are arithmetic (eps(sh2o)/dt = 6.7e-15 per second here) and modelling (the O(dt) difference between WRF's sequential composition and a continuous sum at one state). The measured 4.64e-14 is seven times the arithmetic one, so what 2e-13 is protecting against is a real disagreement between two formulations of the same physics, not a limit on how precisely the reference can be read. The four other frozen-column documents are the other way round -- floor-sized, with the splitting error invisible beneath it. A NOTE ON WHAT THE BOUND MEANS, because it is load-bearing here and was not at first. An esm tolerance of `{abs: x}` ALONE is satisfied by a 1e-6 RELATIVE error -- the runner ORs the absolute bound with a default relative one -- so an absolute bound only binds when `rel: 0.0` is written beside it. Every assertion in this document pins `rel: 0.0`, and the indicators are `{abs: 0.0, rel: 0.0}`, which is genuinely exact rather than exact-looking. Verified by construction: with `rel` left implicit these assertions also pass at `abs: 0`, which is the tell. THIS COLUMN: case B step 1841, a 30 cm pack under warm advection, SNOPAC's MELT branch, and the strongest melt in the cold-season set. The precipitation falls as snow and goes to the pack, so the melt is the entire surface water supply. The frozen sink is held at `sh2o` in the top layer and runs in the other three.
